title: Type-A Hecke Specht Modules and Cellular Bases

items.title: Cellular bases and cell modules
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) which is free as an $R$-module on a finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$, where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set. For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ be the $R$-submodule of $A$ spanned by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$. Then $(C,\Lambda)$ is a **cellular basis** of $A$, and $A$ is a **cellular algebra**, if: (i) the $R$-linear map $i:A\to A$ with $i(c^{\lambda}_{st})=c^{\lambda}_{ts}$ for all $\lambda,s,t$ is an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$, i.e. $i(ab)=i(b)i(a)$ and $i(1)=1$ (equivalently $i$ is an isomorphism of $A$ with the opposite algebra; the displayed formula forces $i^2=\mathrm{id}$); and (ii) for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, every $t\in T(\lambda)$ and every $a\in A$ there exist $r_v\in R$ ($v\in T(\lambda)$) with $$c^{\lambda}_{st}\,a\equiv\sum_{v\in T(\lambda)}r_v\,c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}.$$

**Cell modules.** For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $C^{\lambda}$ be the free $R$-module with basis $\{c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_{tt}:t\in T(\lambda)\}$; condition (ii) makes $C^{\lambda}$ a right $A$-module by $c^{\lambda}_t a:=\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_v$ when $c^{\lambda}_{tt}a\equiv\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$, and it makes $C^{\lambda}$ a left $A$-module via $i$. The module $C^{\lambda}$ is the **(right) cell module** of $\lambda$, and $A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}\cong C^{\lambda}\otimes_R C^{\lambda}$ via $c^{\lambda}_{st}+A^{\rhd\lambda}\mapsto c^{\lambda}_s\otimes c^{\lambda}_t$. A cellular algebra may have several cellular bases.
items.strategy: A definition item recording the Graham-Lehrer axioms exactly as used later. The only point needing care is that the displayed formula really defines a module action: this is Corollary 2.3(i) of the source, obtained by applying the anti-automorphism (i) to the triangular relation; the ideal identification is the display after (2.5). In every application on this page $A=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ is a free $R$-module of finite rank. No choice is used.

Mathas-Soriano, Seminormal forms and Gram determinants for cellular algebras, sections 2.8-2.15 (the Graham-Lehrer axioms in the form used here), pp. 4-7

items.title: e-regular and e-restricted partitions
items.statement: Let $e\in\{2,3,4,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with parts $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots$ and conjugate $\lambda'$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Then $\lambda$ is **$e$-regular** when every positive integer occurs as a part of $\lambda$ fewer than $e$ times, i.e. $z_j(\lambda)<e$ for every $j\ge1$, and **$e$-restricted** when $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ for every $i\ge1$ (with $\lambda_i:=0$ for $i>\ell(\lambda)$). For finite $e$ these are exactly the $p$-regular and $p$-restricted notions of [[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]] with $p=e$, and $\lambda$ is $e$-restricted if and only if its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular. For $e=\infty$ both conditions are vacuous, so every partition is both $e$-regular and $e$-restricted.
items.strategy: A definition item specialising the published $p$-regular/$p$-restricted definitions along the prime $p=e$; the conjugate equivalence is the finite-$e$ case of the corresponding statement for partitions ([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]). No choice is used.

references.title: Mathas, Iwahori-Hecke Algebras and Schur Algebras of the Symmetric Group, the definition of $e$-restricted partitions in Chapter 3 section 4, printed p. 32
Kleshchev, Symmetric groups and related Hecke algebras, section 5.3 (e-restricted labels and Remark 5.5), p. 24

items.title: The quantum characteristic of an invertible Hecke parameter
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{	imes}$ an invertible element. The **quantum characteristic** $e=e(F,q)$ is the least integer $e\ge2$ such that $1+q+\cdots+q^{e-1}=0$ in $F$, and $e:=\infty$ when no such integer exists ([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]], [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Since $[1]_q=1
e0$, the least positive integer $e$ with $[e]_q=0$, when it exists, automatically satisfies $e\ge2$, so the two formulations coincide. Concretely: (i) if $q
e1$ then $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\ge0$, so a finite $e$ exists exactly when $q$ is a root of unity and then $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$ in $F^{	imes}$; (ii) if $q=1$ then $[m]_1=m$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ when $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$ and $e=\infty$ when $\operatorname{char}(F)=0$ ([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]). If $e<\infty$ then $q
e1$ implies $q^e=1$, and hence $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for every integer $m$; in particular the quantum characteristic, not merely the multiplicative order, is the parameter governing the modular representation theory of the Hecke algebra. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: A definition item; the identities $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for $q\ne1$ and $[m]_1=m$ are the definition of the quantum integers, and the displayed equivalences are immediate case checks. The last sentence records the reduction $[m+e]_q=[m]_q+q^m[e]_q$ that every later residue computation uses. No choice is used.

references.title: Mathas, Iwahori-Hecke Algebras and Schur Algebras of the Symmetric Group, (3.28) with the surrounding quantum-integer conventions, printed pp. 27 and 56
Kleshchev, Symmetric groups and related Hecke algebras, section 5.3: the quantum characteristic e, p. 24

items.title: Decompositions of the identity into primitive central idempotents are unique
items.statement: Let $A$ be a unital ring, with centre $Z(A):=\{z\in A: za=az	ext{ for all }a\in A\}$. Suppose that $$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k=f_1+\cdots+f_\ell$$ where $\{e_1,\dots,e_k\}$ and $\{f_1,\dots,f_\ell\}$ are finite families of pairwise orthogonal central idempotents of $A$ that are primitive among central idempotents: each is nonzero and admits no decomposition as a sum of two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents (zero parts are omitted). Then $k=\ell$ and there is a bijection $\sigma$ of the index sets with $e_i=f_{\sigma(i)}$ for all $i$; in particular the decomposition of $1$ into primitive central idempotents is unique up to order. No choice principle is used, the families being finite.
items.strategy: For each pair, $e_if_j$ is an idempotent (all factors commute) and $\sum_j e_if_j=e_i$ with pairwise orthogonal terms; primitivity of $e_i$ forces all but one term to vanish, say $e_i=e_if_{j(i)}$. Symmetrically each $f_j$ admits exactly one $i$ with $f_j=f_je_i$. The map $i\mapsto j(i)$ is injective (otherwise some $f_j$ would split as a sum of two nonzero orthogonal idempotents), and counting the two decompositions of $1$ shows that it is a bijection; then $e_i=e_if_{j(i)}=f_{j(i)}e_i=f_{j(i)}$ because all idempotents involved are central, so the families coincide. No choice is used.

references.title: Andrew Mathas, Iwahori-Hecke Algebras and Schur Algebras of the Symmetric Group, Chapter 5 section 3 (block conventions) and the standard uniqueness of primitive central orthogonal decompositions, printed pp. 53-54
Jacobsen, Block fusion systems and the center of the group ring, sections 1.1 and 2.2 (primitive idempotent decompositions), pp. 3-8 and 13-18

items.title: The identity of a finite-dimensional algebra decomposes into primitive central idempotents
items.statement: Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre $Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az	ext{ for all }a\in A\}$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). Then $Z(A)$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $F$-algebra, and the identity $1\in Z(A)$ admits a decomposition $$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$$ into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents of $A$: each $e_i$ is a nonzero idempotent of $Z(A)$ that is not the sum of two nonzero orthogonal idempotents of $Z(A)$. No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed and no choice principle is used.
items.strategy: A subset of $Z(A)$ that is linearly independent over $F$ is linearly independent in the finite-dimensional space $A$, so it has at most $\dim_FA$ elements and $Z(A)$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $F$-algebra; its idempotents are exactly the central idempotents of $A$. Start with the family $\{1\}$ and split any non-primitive member $e$ as $e=u+v$ with $u,v$ nonzero orthogonal idempotents of $Z(A)$. The corners $uZ(A)u$ and $vZ(A)v$ are subspaces of $eZ(A)e$ of strictly smaller dimension (multiplication by $u$ kills $v$ but fixes $uZ(A)u$), and a mutually orthogonal family of nonzero idempotents is linearly independent, so the process terminates after at most $\dim_FZ(A)$ splits. The terminal family is the asserted decomposition and every member is primitive by construction. This is the standard finite-dimensional dimension-descent argument applied to the centre; the same argument for arbitrary finite-dimensional algebras is recorded in the published literature cited below. No choice is used.

references.title: Mathas, Iwahori-Hecke Algebras and Schur Algebras of the Symmetric Group, Chapter 5 section 3 (block conventions and primitive central idempotents), printed pp. 53-54
Jacobsen, Block fusion systems and the center of the group ring, sections 1.1 and 2.2 (finite-dimensional primitive idempotent decompositions), pp. 3-8 and 13-18

items.title: The star anti-automorphism of the type-A Hecke algebra
items.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ be the specialized type-A Hecke algebra with generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and relations $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$, the braid relations and the distant commutations ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Then the assignment $T_i\mapsto T_i$ ($1\le i<n$) extends uniquely to an $R$-algebra anti-automorphism $*:H\to H$, i.e. an $R$-linear map with $(ab)^*=b^*a^*$ and $1^*=1$; it is an involution, $**=\mathrm{id}_H$, and on the standard basis $$T_w^{*}=T_{w^{-1}}\qquad(w\in S_n).$$ In particular $(T_wT_{w^{-1}})^*=T_wT_{w^{-1}}$ and, for the symmetrizers $m_\lambda=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w$, one has $m_\lambda^*=m_\lambda$.
items.strategy: The presentation ideal of $H$ is stable under reversal of products: the quadratic, braid and distant-commutation relators are palindromic, so the universal property of the presented algebra applied to $H^{\mathrm{op}}$ yields a unique algebra homomorphism $H\to H^{\mathrm{op}}$ sending each $T_i$ to $T_i$, i.e. an anti-automorphism $*$ of $H$. Since $*$ fixes a generating set, $**$ fixes a generating set and hence is the identity. For a reduced word $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$ one has $T_w=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}$ by definition, so $T_w^*=T_{i_\ell}\cdots T_{i_1}=T_{w^{-1}}$, the reversed word being reduced for $w^{-1}$. This is Mathas, Chapter 3 section 2, where $*$ is the $R$-linear antiautomorphism determined by $T_i^*=T_i$ and $T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$; no choice is used.

references.title: Mathas, Iwahori-Hecke Algebras and Schur Algebras of the Symmetric Group, Chapter 3 section 2: the antiautomorphism with $T_i^*=T_i$, $T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$, printed pp. 20-25

items.title: Blocks of a finite-dimensional algebra via primitive central idempotents
items.statement: Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre $Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az	ext{ for all }a\in A\}$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). A **central idempotent** of $A$ is an idempotent $e\in Z(A)$; it is **primitive** when $e\ne0$ and $e$ is not the sum of two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents. Then $Z(A)$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $F$-algebra, so $1\in Z(A)$ admits a decomposition $$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$$ into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents ([[lem-the-identity-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-decomposes-into-primitive-central-idempotents]]), and this decomposition is unique up to order ([[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]). A **block** of $A$ is the two-sided ideal $B=eA=Ae$ cut out by a primitive central idempotent $e$. The blocks are pairwise orthogonal two-sided ideals, $A=B_1\oplus\cdots\oplus B_k$ as $F$-algebras with units $e_i$, each $B_i$ is an indecomposable two-sided ideal, and for every (not necessarily finite-dimensional) $A$-module $M$ one has $M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^ke_iM$ as $A$-modules; a simple $A$-module $S$ satisfies $e_iS\ne0$ for exactly one $i$ and then $S=e_iS$ lies in the corresponding block. Nothing here asserts that a block is semisimple or simple, and the construction is choice-free.
items.strategy: A definition item whose consistency is supplied by its dependencies: the preceding primitive-idempotent decomposition lemma applied to the commutative finite-dimensional $F$-algebra $Z(A)$ produces the primitive central idempotents (its primitive idempotents are exactly the primitive central idempotents of $A$), and the uniqueness lemma makes the block partition canonical. The module decomposition is idempotent calculus: $\sum_ie_i=1$ gives $M=\sum_ie_iM$, orthogonality gives directness, and a nonzero simple $S$ has $e_iS=S$ whenever $e_iS\ne0$. This avoids the Artinian structure theorem and hence uses no choice principle. The conventions follow Mathas, Chapter 5 section 3 (printed pp. 53-54).

references.title: Mathas, Iwahori-Hecke Algebras and Schur Algebras of the Symmetric Group, Chapter 5 section 3 (block conventions for $S(d,n)$ and $H$), printed pp. 53-54
Jacobsen, Block fusion systems and the center of the group ring, sections 1.1 and 2.2 (finite-dimensional primitive idempotent decompositions), pp. 3-8 and 13-18

items.title: Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements and q-contents
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). For $1\le k\le n$ define $$L_1:=0,\qquad L_k:=q^{-1}T_{(k-1,k)}+q^{-2}T_{(k-2,k)}+\cdots+q^{1-k}T_{(1,k)}\in H\quad(k\ge2),$$ where $T_{(i,k)}$ is the standard basis element indexed by the transposition $(i\ k)$ ([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). The $L_k$ are the **Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements**. They are fixed by the star anti-automorphism $T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$ ([[lem-the-star-antiautomorphism-of-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); they commute pairwise and every symmetric polynomial in $L_1,\dots,L_n$ with coefficients in $R$ is central in $H$ ([[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]).

**q-contents.** The quantum integers $[m]_q$ for $m\ge0$ are those of [[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]; extend the definition to negative indices by $[-m]_q:=-q^{-m}[m]_q$ for $m>0$, so that $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\in\mathbb Z$ when $q\ne1$, and $[m]_1=m$ for all $m\in\mathbb Z$. For a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ and $1\le k\le n$ let $\operatorname{content}_t(k)=c-r$ be the content of the node carrying $k$ ([[def-content-vector-of-a-standard-tableau]]) and define the **q-content value** $[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$. If $e=e(F,q)<\infty$ for a field $F$ then $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for every $m\in\mathbb Z$, so the q-content value depends only on the residue of the content modulo $e$. At $q=1$ the specialization $T_w\mapsto w$ of [[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]] sends $L_k$ to the ordinary Jucys-Murphy element $X_k=\sum_{j<k}(j\ k)$ ([[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]), and $[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_1=\operatorname{content}_t(k)$.
items.strategy: A definition item. Star-invariance is immediate from $T_{(i,k)}^*=T_{(i,k)}$ and the symmetry of the coefficients; commutation and centrality are deferred to [[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]; the $q=1$ limit is the substitution $q^{i-k}\mapsto1$ followed by $T_{(i,k)}\mapsto(i\ k)$. The negative-index extension is the standard convention of the source (3.27). No choice is used.

references.title: Mathas, Iwahori-Hecke Algebras and Schur Algebras of the Symmetric Group, the definition of $L_k$, (3.27)-(3.28) and Corollary 3.25, printed pp. 26-28
Mathas-Soriano, Seminormal forms and Gram determinants for cellular algebras, section 2.15 (the Hecke JM family and q-contents), pp. 6-7

items.title: Murphy elements and Murphy tableau elements
items.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ with standard basis $\{T_w\}$ and star anti-automorphism $*$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], [[lem-the-star-antiautomorphism-of-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). For a composition (in particular a partition) $\mu$ of $n$ put $m_\mu:=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w\in H$, the **row symmetrizer** of the standard Young subgroup $S_\mu$ ([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]); the sum has $|S_\mu|=\prod_i\mu_i!$ terms. For a row-standard $\mu$-tableau $s$ ([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]) let $d(s)\in S_n$ be the unique permutation of minimal length with $s=t^{\mu}d(s)$, where $t^{\mu}$ is the row-standard tableau obtained by entering $1,2,\dots,n$ in increasing order from left to right along the rows; $d(s)$ is the distinguished right-coset representative of $S_\mu$ in $S_n$ and $S_\mu$ is the stabiliser of $t^\mu$ ([[def-row-and-column-stabilizers-of-a-tableau]]). For row-standard $\mu$-tableaux $s,t$ define the **Murphy element** $$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^{*}\,m_{\mu}\,T_{d(t)}\in H,$$ and for a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ shorten $m_t:=m_{tt}=T_{d(t)}^{*}m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$. Then $m_{st}^{*}=m_{ts}$ for all row-standard $s,t$ of the same shape, and $m_\mu T_w=q^{\ell(w)}m_\mu$ for every $w\in S_\mu$.
items.strategy: A definition item. The existence and uniqueness of $d(s)$, and the identity $\ell(wd)=\ell(w)+\ell(d)$ for $w\in S_\mu$, $d\in D_\mu$, are Proposition 3.3 and Corollary 3.4 of the source; $m_\mu T_w=q^{\ell(w)}m_\mu$ is Lemma 3.2, and the symmetry $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$ is immediate from $**=\mathrm{id}$. No choice is used.

references.title: Mathas, Iwahori-Hecke Algebras and Schur Algebras of the Symmetric Group, Chapter 3 sections 1-2: Lemma 3.2, Proposition 3.3, Corollary 3.4 and the definition of $m_{st}$, printed pp. 18-21

items.title: The cell form is associative and its radical is a submodule
items.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $A$ a cellular $R$-algebra with cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ and cell modules $C^{\lambda}$ ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For each $\lambda\in\Lambda$ there is a unique $R$-bilinear form $$\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:C^{\lambda}\times C^{\lambda}\longrightarrow R$$ with $$c^{\lambda}_{us}c^{\lambda}_{tv}\equiv\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$$ for all $s,t,u,v\in T(\lambda)$; in particular the right hand side is independent of $u$ and $v$, and $\langle c^{\lambda}_s,c^{\lambda}_t\rangle_\lambda$ depends only on $s,t$. This form is (i) symmetric, $\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle y,x\rangle_\lambda$; (ii) associative, $\langle xa,y\rangle_\lambda=\langle x,\,i(a)y\rangle_\lambda$ for all $a\in A$ (and dually for the left action); (iii) characterised by $x\,c^{\lambda}_{uv}=\langle x,c^{\lambda}_u\rangle_\lambda\,c^{\lambda}_v$ for $x\in C^{\lambda}$; and (iv) its radical $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}:=\{x\in C^{\lambda}:\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda=0\text{ for all }y\in C^{\lambda}\}$ is an $A$-submodule of $C^{\lambda}$, namely the kernel of $x\mapsto\langle x,-\rangle_\lambda$.
items.strategy: Uniqueness and independence of $u,v$: multiply $c^{\lambda}_{us}c^{\lambda}_{tv}$ on the left by $c^{\lambda}_{wu}$ and compare the two resulting expressions inside the free quotient $A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}$ using (2.1). Symmetry: apply the anti-automorphism $i$ to $c^{\lambda}_{us}c^{\lambda}_{tv}\equiv\langle c_s,c_t\rangle c_{uv}$ and use the stability of $A^{\rhd\lambda}$. Associativity is the comparison of the two ways to associate $c^{\lambda}_{us}(c^{\lambda}_{tv}a)$ modulo $A^{\rhd\lambda}$. For (iv), (iii) shows that for fixed $y$ the map $x\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle_\lambda$ is $A$-linear where defined, so its kernel is a submodule; the radical is the intersection of these kernels. This is Mathas, Corollary 2.3(iv), (2.6), Proposition 2.7 and Lemma 2.8, printed pp. 10-11; no choice is used.

references.title: Mathas, Iwahori-Hecke Algebras and Schur Algebras of the Symmetric Group, Corollary 2.3(iv), (2.6), Proposition 2.7, Lemma 2.8, printed pp. 10-11
Mathas-Soriano, Seminormal forms and Gram determinants for cellular algebras, sections 3.1-3.7 (cell forms and their radicals), pp. 9-11

items.title: The type-A q-Schur algebra and its Weyl modules
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{	imes}$, $d,n\ge0$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Let $\Lambda(d,n)$ be the set of compositions $\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_d)$ of $n$ (so $\mu_i\in\mathbb N$ and $\sum_i\mu_i=n$). For $\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)$ let $m_\mu=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w$ ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]) and let $M^{\mu}:=m_\mu H$ be the right ideal it generates, the **(Hecke) permutation module**; $M^{\mu}$ is free over $R$ with basis $\{m_\mu T_{d(t)}:t	ext{ row-standard }\mu	ext{-tableau}\}$ and is the Hecke analogue of the module induced from the trivial representation of the Young subgroup ([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]).

Here is the freeness statement in detail: the cosets $S_\mu d$ with $d\in D_\mu$ partition $S_n$, and $\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$ for $u\in S_\mu$, $d\in D_\mu$ ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), so the standard basis theorem ([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]) gives $T_uT_{d(t)}=T_{ud(t)}$ and $m_\mu T_{d(t)}=\sum_{u\in S_\mu}T_{u\,d(t)}$; these are the standard basis elements indexed by the single coset $S_\mu d(t)$, and the cosets are disjoint, whence $M^\mu= igoplus_tR\,m_\mu T_{d(t)}$ is free with the displayed basis as $t$ runs over the row-standard $\mu$-tableaux.

items.title: The Murphy tableau elements form a cellular basis
items.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Let $\Lambda$ be the set of partitions of $n$ ordered by dominance $\unrhd$ ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]), and for $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $T(\lambda)=\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$ be the set of standard $\lambda$-tableaux ([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$, let $q\in R^{\times}$, let $d,n\ge0$ with $d\ge n$, and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write $S:=S(d,n)=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for the type-A q-Schur algebra with $M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ the direct sum of the permutation modules ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and let $\{\varphi_{ST}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n),\ S,T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$ be its cellular semistandard basis ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]] for the underlying Murphy elements and [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] for the standard basis along which this basis is defined). Put $\omega:=(1^n)\in\Lambda(d,n)$, the composition with $n$ parts equal to $1$ (legitimate because $d\ge n$), so that the Young subgroup $S_\omega$ is trivial and $m_\omega=1$; hence $$M^{\omega}=m_\omega H=H$$ is the regular right $H$-module. Let $t^{\omega}$ be the unique standard $\omega$-tableau, with entries $1,2,\dots,n$ down its single column; it is in particular the unique row-standard $\omega$-tableau whose entries increase down the column. Set $$e:=\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}\in S.$$

Then:

1. $e$ is the projection of $M$ onto the direct summand $M^{\omega}=H$ along the other summands $M^{\mu}$, $\mu\ne\omega$; in particular $e^2=e$ and $$eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})=\mathrm{End}_H(H),$$ via the algebra isomorphism $$\rho:H\longrightarrow eSe,\qquad h\longmapsto\rho_h,\qquad \rho_h(x):=hx,$$ left multiplication by $h$ on $M^{\omega}=H$ being a right $H$-module endomorphism. Here the isomorphism $eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})$ sends $efe$ to $f|_{M^{\omega}}$ and is inverted by extending an endomorphism of $M^{\omega}$ by zero on the other summands, and the identification $\mathrm{End}_H(H)\cong H$ sends an endomorphism to its value at $1$. By the construction of the semistandard basis elements $\varphi_{ST}$ (Mathas (4.13) with Corollaries 4.9 and 4.12; see the locator above), the diagonal element $\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ is exactly the endomorphism of $M$ that is the identity on $M^{\omega}$ and zero on all $M^{\mu}$ with $\mu\ne\omega$, which is the projection asserted above. 2. The **Schur functor** is $$F:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}S\longrightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}H,\qquad F(X):=Xe=X\otimes_SSe,$$ with the right $H$-action transported along $\rho$, so that $(xe)\cdot h:=x\,\rho_h$ for $x\in X$, $h\in H$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). It is exact and $R$-linear on morphisms: as a **left** $S$-module, $Se$ is the image of the left-$S$-linear projection $s\mapsto se$ on $S$, hence is a direct summand of the regular left module and is projective. Tensoring right $S$-modules with this left module is therefore exact. Equivalently, for a short exact sequence of right modules, an element $ye$ in the target lifts to $xe$ from any lift $x$ of $y$; kernels and injections are likewise preserved by the same idempotent projection. The bimodule corner action makes these maps right $H$-linear. The convention is fixed: the functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ on the right, and the left-module formula $X\mapsto eX$ is not used on this page.

items.title: The type-A Hecke Specht module and its cell form
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $q\in R^{\times}$. With the Murphy cellular basis $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]], [[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) and the canonical tableau $t^\lambda$ of shape $\lambda\vdash n$ ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), the **Murphy cell module** $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the right cell module $C^{\lambda}$ of the Murphy basis: it is the free $R$-module with basis $\{m_t:=m_{t^\lambda t}:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ - the classes of the Murphy elements whose *first* index is the canonical tableau - and $H$ acts by $m_th=\sum_vr_vm_v$ whenever $m_{t^\lambda t}h\equiv\sum_vr_vm_{t^\lambda v}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$. (The cellular action rule transforms the second index and fixes the first, so the diagonal elements $m_{tt}$ alone do not span a submodule; the explicit failure for $\lambda=(2,1)$ is recorded in the proof strategy.) Its **cell form** is the unique bilinear form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\times S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\to R$ with $$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv\langle m_s,m_t\rangle_\lambda\,m_{uv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$$ for all $s,t,u,v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$; it is symmetric and associative and $\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is a submodule, so $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}:=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is a right $H$-module ([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]).

**Convention (Dipper-James signed cellular normalization).** Let $\theta:H\to H$ be the involutive algebra automorphism defined by $\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}=(q-1)-T_i$. For a right module $M$, write $M^\theta$ for the same $R$-module with action $x\cdot h=x\theta(h)$. The page's ordinary Specht normalization is the signed conjugate Murphy construction
$$S^{\lambda}:=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta.$$
Its form is the form of $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ on the same underlying module; because $\theta$ commutes with $*$ this is associative for the twisted action. Over a field put
$$D^{\lambda}:=S^{\lambda}/\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}S^{\lambda}=(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta.$$
Thus $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(S^{\lambda})^\theta$ and $D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(D^{\lambda})^\theta$; conjugation alone does not identify these modules. At $q=1$, $\theta(\sigma)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\sigma$, so these identities contain tensoring with sign. In characteristic $2$ the sign twist becomes trivial at $q=1$. The nonzero quotients in this signed normalization have $e$-regular labels because the nonzero Murphy quotients have conjugate $e$-restricted labels. No generic root-of-unity Hecke claim is inferred from the published prime-characteristic group-only sign dictionary. No semisimplicity or choice principle is assumed.

items.title: The Jantzen filtration of a lifted cell module
items.statement: Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain ([[def-principal-ideal-domain]]) with a chosen prime element $\pi$, let $F:=R/\pi R$ be the residue field, and let $M$ be a free $R$-module of finite rank ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]) equipped with a symmetric $R$-bilinear form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle:M\times M\to R$ whose extension to the fraction field $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ is non-degenerate (equivalently $\det G\ne0$ for a Gram matrix $G$ of the form). For $i\ge1$ put $$M(i):=\{x\in M:\langle x,y\rangle\in\pi^iR\ \text{for all }y\in M\},\qquad M_F(i):=(M(i)+\pi M)/\pi M\subseteq M_F:=M\otimes_RF.$$ Then $M(0)=M$, the $M(i)$ are $R$-submodules with $M(i+1)\subseteq M(i)$, the descending chain $$M_F=M_F(0)\supseteq M_F(1)\supseteq M_F(2)\supseteq\cdots$$ stabilises at $0$ (that is, $M_F(z)=0$ for all sufficiently large $z$, because $\det G\ne0$), and $M_F(1)=\mathrm{rad}\,M_F$, the radical of the reduced form. This finite descending filtration is the **Jantzen filtration** of $M$ with respect to $(R,\pi,\langle\ ,\ \rangle)$. The hypotheses are exactly: $R$ a PID, $\pi$ a prime element, the form non-degenerate over $\operatorname{Frac}(R)$; no valuation-ring or DVR hypothesis is substituted, and the prime element $\pi$, its ideal $\pi R$ and the fraction field $K$ are kept distinct.
items.strategy: A definition item. Each $M(i)$ is a submodule: for the cell forms on this page the associativity identity $\langle xa,y\rangle=\langle x,ya^*\rangle$ shows closedness under the action. Reduction gives a descending chain of finite-dimensional $F$-spaces, so it stabilises; $\det G\ne0$ makes the stable value $0$ because a vector whose pairing with every basis vector lies in all $\pi^iR$ is zero over $K$. Finally $x\in M(1)$ reduces into the radical of the reduced form by definition. This is Mathas, Chapter 5 section 2 (setup preceding Lemma 5.29), printed pp. 54-55; no choice is used.

items.title: The Hecke Jucys-Murphy action is dominance triangular
items.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, and let $L_1,\dots,L_n$ be the Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements ([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]). For every $\lambda\vdash n$, every standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ and every $1\le k\le n$ there exist $a_v\in R$ with $$m_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q\,m_t+\sum_{v\rhd t}a_v\,m_v,$$ where $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ is the Murphy basis of the Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) and the sum is over standard $\lambda$-tableaux $v$ strictly dominating $t$ in the dominance order on tableaux ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]], [[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). In particular $L_k$ acts on the Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ with Murphy basis $(m_t)$ by a triangular matrix whose diagonal entries are the q-content values. Consequently the $L_k$ commute pairwise and every symmetric polynomial in $L_1,\dots,L_n$ is central in $H$.
items.strategy: Induct on $n$ and then on $k$ exactly as in the source. If $k$ lies in a non-last row of $t$, delete the last row and apply the induction hypothesis to the smaller partition; if $k$ is not in the first column, use $m_tL_k=m_t(1+L_{k-1}T_{k-1})$ together with the induction on $k$ and the quadratic relation; the remaining case (last row and first column) is handled by writing $m_t=hm_{\mu'}$ with $\mu'=(\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_r,1)$ and applying the Garnir relation Lemma 3.31 plus the induction hypothesis. This is Mathas, Theorem 3.30 (Dipper-James) with Proposition 3.24 and Corollary 3.25. No choice is used.

items.title: The simple type-A Hecke modules are indexed by e-regular partitions
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, let $e=e(F,q)\in\{2,3,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ be the quantum characteristic ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]) and let $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for $n\ge0$. For $\lambda\vdash n$ let $S^{\lambda}$ be the Hecke Specht module and $D^{\lambda}=S^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}$ its cell-form quotient ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]). Then:

1. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if $\lambda$ is $e$-regular ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]); 2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\vdash n\text{ is }e\text{-regular}\}$ is a complete set of pairwise non-isomorphic absolutely irreducible $H$-modules; 3. $H$ is split semisimple if and only if $e>n$ (including $e=\infty$); when $e\le n$ the algebra has nonzero radical.

This is the exact root-of-unity replacement for the ordinary Specht classification. At $q=1$ in characteristic $p>0$ it specialises to the classification of the simple $F[S_n]$-modules by $p$-regular partitions ([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]). No semisimplicity is assumed and no choice principle is used.

## Statement

Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, let $e=e(F,q)\in\{2,3,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ be the quantum characteristic ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]) and let $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for $n\ge0$. For $\lambda\vdash n$ let $S^{\lambda}$ be the Hecke Specht module and $D^{\lambda}=S^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}$ its cell-form quotient ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]). At $q=1$ in characteristic $p>0$ it specialises to the classification of the simple $F[S_n]$-modules by $p$-regular partitions ([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]). No semisimplicity is assumed and no choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, $q\in F^{\times}$, the algebra $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$, its Hecke Specht modules $S^{\lambda}$ and quotients $D^{\lambda}$ in the signed conjugate normalization ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]), and the numbers $e(F,q)$ and $[\ ]_q$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]).

[F1] ([[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]) The nonzero $D^{\lambda}$ form a complete set of pairwise non-isomorphic absolutely irreducible $H$-modules; $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form on $S^{\lambda}$ is not identically zero.

[F2] ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) In the signed conjugate normalization $S^{\lambda}=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$ and $D^{\lambda}=(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, where $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ is the Murphy cell module, $\theta$ is the involutive automorphism with $\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}=(q-1)-T_i$, and pullback along $\theta$ is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, nonzero modules and simplicity.

[F3] The complete relevant source proof is Mathas, Lemmas 3.35, 3.37, 3.38 and Theorem 3.39, printed pp. 32-34 (PDF pp. 38-40 of the guarded 79-page manuscript). The residue-character lower bound, ladder argument and **common factor of every Gram entry** are given explicitly below. The common factor is not a Gram determinant, and no full-hook product formula for all Specht determinants is asserted.

[F4] ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]) $\lambda$ is $e$-regular if and only if its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-restricted.

[F5] ([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]) At $q=1$ in characteristic $p>0$ the simple $F[S_n]$-modules are the heads of the Specht modules for the $p$-regular partitions.





## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Work first with Murphy cells $C^\eta=S_{\mathrm M}^\eta$ and their quotients $D_{\mathrm M}^\eta$. Their Jucys-Murphy action is triangular in the standard-tableau basis by [[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]. The cell-order multiplicity and diagonal-purity facts used here are [[cor-cellular-decomposition-matrices-are-dominance-unitriangular]]; the independent integral Murphy basis/straightening supplies the row-symmetrizer calculation via [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-integral-murphy-and-polytabloid-straightening]]. Thus restriction to the commutative algebra $\mathbb L$ generated by these elements has a one-dimensional-factor filtration, with the character of tableau $t$ given by the tuple $([\operatorname{res}_t(1)]_q,\ldots,[\operatorname{res}_t(n)]_q)$. Call a tableau of shape $\eta$ restricted if its tuple occurs in no standard tableau of a strictly smaller shape in the Murphy cell order. Cellularity gives $[C^\eta:D_{\mathrm M}^\rho]=0$ unless $\eta\unrhd\rho$ and gives diagonal multiplicity $1$ when the labelled quotient is nonzero. A restricted-tableau character therefore cannot be accounted for by any strictly smaller labelled simple. Every copy of such a character in $C^\eta|_{\mathbb L}$ must lie in its one diagonal copy of $D_{\mathrm M}^\eta|_{\mathbb L}$. Additivity of finite character multiplicities gives $$\dim D_{\mathrm M}^\eta\ge   |\operatorname{Std}_e(\eta)|.$$ This is the full residue-character argument of Mathas Lemma 3.35; it does not infer a nonzero labelled quotient merely from the existence of an unspecified composition factor. [F1, F3, given]

1.2 For the converse, carry out the row-symmetrizer calculation over the universal Laurent domain $A=\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$, then specialize $Q$ to $q$. For $\eta=(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_k)$ put $\delta^i=(\eta_i-\eta_{i+1},\ldots,\eta_k)$, of total size $\eta_i$. Let $g_i$ be the greatest common divisor of $[\gamma]!_Q$ over partitions $\gamma\vdash\eta_i$ dominating this row-difference composition, and put $g^\eta=\prod_i g_i$. The rowwise calculation shows that every cell-form entry is divisible by $g^\eta$. Here is the calculation, rather than a claim about the determinant. [given, F3]

2.1 If finite $e$ and $\eta$ is $e$-restricted, give the node $(a,b)$ ladder number $a+(e-1)b-e$. To construct the ladder tableau, place the last entry in a removable node of maximum ladder number, choosing the uppermost such node, and repeat on the remaining diagram. Removing this node leaves an $e$-restricted partition: increasing the preceding row difference to $e$ would put a node of greater ladder number in that preceding row, contradicting the choice; the other potentially changed difference cannot reach $e$ from a restricted partition. The chosen node is the lowest addable node with its residue compatible with the required dominance comparison. Induct on the number of entries: if a tableau of shape $\rho\unlhd\eta$ has the same residue tuple, the truncated shapes still have the required dominance comparison. The induction hypothesis forces the truncated tableau to equal the smaller ladder tableau. Its final node has the same residue; the extremal-node choice and dominance force that node to be the chosen one. Thus $\rho=\eta$ and the whole tableau is the ladder tableau. In particular this tableau is restricted. Step 1.1 then proves $D_{\mathrm M}^\eta\ne0$. This is Mathas Lemma 3.37 with its entire induction, completed on printed p. 33. [F3, step 1.1]

2.2 Write $x_\eta=x_{\eta_1}\cdots x_{\eta_k}$, the row symmetrizers on successive row intervals. For a row-standard tableau $t$, count the entries $1,\ldots,\eta_1$ in its rows; call their composition $\beta$. Sort these entries in reading order without changing the others, obtaining $u$ with $t=uw$, $w\in S_{\eta_1}$ and additive Coxeter length. The parabolic coset identity gives $$m_t x_{\eta_1}=Q^{\ell(w)}[\beta]!_Q\,m_u h$$ for some $h$ in the first-row parabolic algebra. The resulting permutation summand has row composition $(\eta_1,\eta_1-\beta_1,\ldots,\eta_k-\beta_k)$. If it is not dominated by $\eta$, its contribution is in the strictly higher Murphy ideal and vanishes in this cell. Otherwise the partial-sum inequalities give $\beta\unrhd\delta^1$, so $g_1$ divides $[\beta]!_Q$ (the reordered partition dominates $\beta$ and has the same factorial). Straighten while keeping the first row fixed: only tableaux agreeing with the canonical first row remain. Repeat the identical argument on the remaining rows. After row $i$ the common factor is $g_1\cdots g_i$ and all surviving tableaux agree with the first $i$ canonical rows. At $i=k$ only the canonical tableau remains. Hence $x_\eta T_{d(t)}x_\eta$ has coefficient divisible by $g^\eta$ on $x_\eta$ modulo higher shapes. The product definition of the cell form therefore makes every Gram entry divisible by $g^\eta$. This is Mathas Lemma 3.38, including its final row-induction step on printed p. 34. [F3, step 1.2]

2.3 For $e>n$, including $e=\infty$, no two distinct standard tableaux have the same residue tuple. Indeed, at the first unequal step their preceding diagram has size $m-1$; its distinct addable-corner contents have nonzero difference of absolute value at most $m\le n$. The identity $[a]_q-[b]_q=q^b[a-b]_q$ makes their residues distinct. Induction recovers the whole tableau and shape from the tuple. Thus all tableaux are restricted in the sense of step 1.1, giving $\dim D_{\mathrm M}^\eta\ge|\operatorname{Std}(\eta)|= \dim C^\eta$. As the quotient cannot have larger dimension, equality holds and every Murphy form has zero radical. This also proves the nonzero criterion at $e=\infty$, where every partition is restricted. [given, step 1.1]

3.1 If $\eta$ is not $e$-restricted, choose $i$ with $\eta_i-\eta_{i+1}\ge e$. Every partition $\gamma$ in the definition of $g_i$ has $\gamma_1\ge\eta_i-\eta_{i+1}\ge e$, so $[e]!_Q$ divides every $[\gamma]!_Q$ and hence divides their gcd $g_i$. It divides $g^\eta$. After specialization, $[e]!_q=0$ and every Gram entry vanishes by step 2.2. Thus the form is identically zero and $D_{\mathrm M}^\eta=0$. Together with step 2.1 this proves the finite-$e$ Murphy criterion. The empty partition at $n=0$ has the one-dimensional unit cell directly. [F3, step 2.1, step 2.2]

3.2 Derive split semisimplicity without the erroneous hook-determinant shortcut. Put $f_\eta=\dim C^\eta$ and $d_\eta=\dim D_{\mathrm M}^\eta$, with $d_\eta=0$ when that quotient is zero. The cellular basis gives $\dim H=\sum_\eta f_\eta^2$. On each nonzero quotient, the nondegenerate quotient form and the cell multiplication rule supply every rank-one operator, so $H\to\operatorname{End}_F(D_{\mathrm M}^\eta)$ is surjective. These kernels are distinct maximal two-sided ideals because the simple modules are pairwise nonisomorphic; the Chinese remainder theorem makes the product map surjective. Its kernel is the intersection of annihilators of all simple modules, namely $\operatorname{rad}H$ by the complete cellular classification. Hence $$\dim(H/\operatorname{rad}H)=\sum_\eta d_\eta^2.$$ When $e>n$, step 2.3 gives $d_\eta=f_\eta$ for every shape, so the kernel is zero and $H$ is a product of full matrix algebras over $F$. When finite $e\le n$, the **Murphy** row cell $(n)$ has form norm $\sum_{w\in S_n}q^{\ell(w)}=[n]!_q=0$, by $x_{(n)}^2=[n]!_q x_{(n)}$. Its quotient is zero but its dimension is $1$. Since $d_\eta\le f_\eta$ for every other shape, the displayed dimension sum is strictly smaller than $\dim H$, so $\operatorname{rad}H\ne0$. The ordinary row Specht is not used as a degenerate example: its normalization is the signed conjugate Murphy cell. This proves part 3. [F1, F2, step 2.3]

4.1 Translate the criterion by the actual signed-conjugate Definition: $D^\lambda=(D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda'})^\theta$. Exact involutive pullback preserves nonzero modules. Thus $D^\lambda\ne0$ precisely when $\lambda'$ is restricted, equivalently when $\lambda$ is regular. The nonzero Murphy quotients are absolutely simple and exhaust the simple modules; applying the same automorphism to all of them preserves these properties. This proves parts 1 and 2. At $q=1$ the actual all-field polytabloid/form bridge gives the group convention, and $e=p$ in positive characteristic. Part 1 then specializes exactly to the published $p$-regular classification. No statement that every zero-form Specht is reducible is made, and no choice principle is used. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 3.1, step 2.3] ∎

## Statement

Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, $e=e(F,q)$ and $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]). For $\lambda\vdash n$ and $e$-regular $\mu\vdash n$ let $$d_{\lambda\mu}:=[S^{\lambda}:D^{\mu}],$$ the multiplicity of $D^{\mu}$ in a composition series of the Specht module $S^{\lambda}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]). Then $$d_{\mu\mu}=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0\ \Longrightarrow\ \mu\unrhd\lambda,$$ where $\unrhd$ is the dominance order on partitions ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]): a simple factor $D^{\mu}$ of $S^{\lambda}$ can occur only if the $e$-regular label $\mu$ dominates $\lambda$. Equivalently the decomposition matrix $(d_{\lambda\mu})$ is unitriangular along dominance. This constrains but does not compute the entries: no off-diagonal decomposition number is determined by cellularity.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, $q\in F^{\times}$, $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ with Specht modules $S^{\lambda}$ and simple quotients $D^{\mu}$ in the signed conjugate normalization ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]), together with the dominance order on partitions of $n$ ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]).

[F1] ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) $S^{\lambda}=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$ and $D^{\mu}=(D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$ for the conjugate partitions, where $S^{\nu}_{\mathrm M}$ is the Murphy cell module and $\theta$ is the involutive automorphism $\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}$; pullback along $\theta$ is exact and preserves submodules, quotients, composition multiplicities and simplicity.

[F2] ([[cor-cellular-decomposition-matrices-are-dominance-unitriangular]]) For the Murphy cellular basis of $H$ the composition multiplicity $[S^{\nu}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}]$ satisfies $[S^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}]=1$ for nonzero $D^{\rho}_{\mathrm M}$ and is zero unless $\nu\unrhd\rho$.

[F3] ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]) Conjugation reverses dominance: $\lambda'\unrhd\mu'$ if and only if $\mu\unrhd\lambda$.

[F4] ([[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]) $D^{\mu}\ne0$ exactly for the $e$-regular $\mu$.



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Invariance of composition multiplicities under the normalisation: by [F1] the twist $(-)^\theta$ is an exact equivalence of module categories with inverse $(-)^\theta$ itself, so it is additive on short exact sequences and carries composition series to composition series; hence $[S^{\lambda}:D^{\mu}]=[S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]$ for all $\lambda\vdash n$ and $e$-regular $\mu\vdash n$. [given, F1, F4]

2.1 Vanishing: if $d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0$, then $[S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]\ne0$ by step 1.1, so $\lambda'\unrhd\mu'$ by [F2], and conjugation reversal [F3] gives $\mu\unrhd\lambda$. [step 1.1, F2, F3]

2.2 Diagonal: taking $\lambda=\mu$ in step 1.1 gives $d_{\mu\mu}=[S^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}:D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]=1$ by [F2]. [step 1.1, F2]

3.1 Assembly: steps 2.1 and 2.2 are exactly the two claims; ordering the rows and columns of $(d_{\lambda\mu})$ by any linear extension of dominance displays the unitriangular shape, and no off-diagonal entry is determined by the cellular structure. At $q=1$ the statement specialises to the classical symmetric-group unitriangularity of [[thm-symmetric-group-decomposition-matrix-is-dominance-unitriangular]] by [F4]. [step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

items.title: Jantzen layer dimensions sum to the Gram determinant valuation
items.statement:
In the setting of [[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]] ($R$ a PID, $\pi$ a prime element, $F=R/\pi R$, $M$ free of finite rank with a form whose extension to $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ is non-degenerate), let $
u_\pi$ be the $\pi$-adic valuation normalised by $
u_\pi(\pi)=1$ and let $G\in R\setminus\{0\}$ be the Gram determinant of the form with respect to any $R$-basis of $M$. Then $$
u_\pi(G)=\sum_{i>0}\dim_FM_F(i),$$ where $M_F(i)$ are the Jantzen layers of [[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]]; in particular the sum is finite and independent of the chosen basis.

Then $G=\pm\prod_ir_i$, so $
u_\pi(G)=\sum_i
u_\pi(r_i)$. On the other hand $x=\sum_ia_ie_i$ lies in $M(k)$ if and only if $
u_\pi(a_ir_i)\ge k$ for all $i$, so $M_F(k)$ has as basis the images of those $e_i$ with $
u_\pi(r_i)\ge k$; hence $\dim_FM_F(k)=\#\{i:
u_\pi(r_i)\ge k\}$ and $\sum_{k>0}\dim_FM_F(k)=\sum_i
u_\pi(r_i)$. This is Mathas, Lemma 5.29 (Jantzen), printed p. 58; no choice is used.

items.title: Hecke Specht theory specialises to group Specht theory at q = 1
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q=1\in F$, and let $H_{F,1}(S_n)$ be the specialization of the generic type-A Hecke algebra at $v\mapsto1$, so that $H_{F,1}(S_n)\cong F[S_n]$ with $T_w\mapsto w$ ([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]). Then the Hecke theory of this page specializes as follows.
1. The Murphy elements $m_\mu=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w$ specialize to the row symmetrizers $\sum_{w\in S_\mu}w$, and the Murphy basis $\{m_{st}\}$ of $H_{F,1}(S_n)$ specializes to the Murphy basis of the group algebra $F[S_n]$ (the base change $\mathbb Z[S_n]\to F[S_n]$ of the integral Murphy basis).
2. For every $\lambda\vdash n$ the specialization of the page's Hecke Specht module $S^{\lambda}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) is the ordinary Specht module in the Dipper-James convention: $S^{\lambda}_{q=1}\cong S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ as $F[S_n]$-modules, with the standard polytabloid basis ([[thm-standard-polytabloid-basis]]); the specialized cell form is the standard bilinear form on $S^{\lambda}_k$ whose radical defines the James quotient $D^{\lambda}$ ([[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]]).
3. The quantum characteristic of $q=1$ is $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ when $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$, and $e=\infty$ when $\operatorname{char}(F)=0$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]); in characteristic $p>0$ a partition is $e$-regular exactly when it is $p$-regular. Hence $D^{\lambda}_{q=1}\ne0$ exactly for $p$-regular $\lambda$ ([[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]), and for non-$p$-regular $\lambda$ one has $\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}=S^{\lambda}$. This matches the group-side classification [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]] and the conjugate-sign dictionary [[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]. In characteristic $0$ the specialization is split semisimple and all Specht modules are irreducible.
items.strategy: Base-change the Murphy cellular basis along $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to F$, $v\mapsto1$: the structure constants are polynomials in $q$, so specialization gives a cellular basis of $F[S_n]$, and the cell modules specialize to the modules with the specialized triangular multiplication. For the ordinary module and form identification, use the actual signed-conjugate comparison of [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]] and its all-field specialization [[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]], through [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]. The base-change compatible map identifies the ordinary polytabloid module with the signed conjugate Murphy cell module, and its explicit Laurent-unit form factor is $q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}$, which equals $1$ at $q=1$ over every field. Thus the ordinary module and standard form agree at this specialization, including zero-form quotients; the printed p. 25 untwisted convention warning is not a proof premise. The simple-label statement is the specialization of [[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]] at $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$, compared with [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]. The direction of information is one-way (this item imports the group classification and no group-side item depends on the Hecke theory). No choice is used.

items.title: The q-Schur Weyl weight-space Gram determinant is a hook product
items.statement:
Let $R$ be an integral domain, $q\in R^\times$, $d,n\ge1$, and let $W^\lambda$ be the Weyl module of $S(d,n)$ for a partition $\lambda\vdash n$ with at most $d$ parts. For a composition $\mu$ of $n$ of length $d$, let $G^\lambda_\mu$ be the Gram determinant of its $\mu$-weight space in the semistandard basis ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Put $\beta_j=\lambda'_j+n-j$ and $h_{ab}=\lambda_a-b+\lambda'_b-a+1$. Then $$G^\lambda_\mu=q^N\prod_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\\b<c}}  \left(\frac{[h_{ab}]_q}{[h_{ac}]_q}\right)^{  d_\mu(\beta+h_{ac}\mathbf e_b-h_{ac}\mathbf e_c)},$$ where $N=\sum_{T\in T_0(\lambda,\mu)}\ell(d(\operatorname{last}(T)))$. Here $\operatorname{last}(T)$ is the least-dominant standardization in the fiber of $T$, and $d_\mu$ is the exact alternating semistandard number of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. **Both beta shifts use the same removed hook length $h_{ac}$.**

The exponent is the sorting sign times $|T_0(\eta,\mu)|$ if that balanced beta sequence has distinct nonnegative entries and recovers $\eta$; it is zero otherwise. Equivalently, remove the rim strip $R_{ac}$ and rewrap its $h_{ac}$ boxes with lowest node in column $b$. The sign is the parity of the heights of the removed strip and the newly added strip, the latter measured in the new diagram $\eta$; it is not generally the sum of two old $\lambda$ hook legs ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]], [[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]).

Form the product first in the universal field $\mathbb Q(Q)$. It equals a Laurent polynomial in $\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$, namely the universal integral Gram determinant divided by its displayed unit $Q^N$. Over $R$ the formula means the specialization of that Laurent polynomial. It does not require inverting a vanishing hook number or evaluating $0/0$. All weights and $d<n$ are retained; an empty weight space has determinant $1$.

## Statement

Let $R$ be an integral domain, $q\in R^\times$, $d,n\ge1$, and let $W^\lambda$ be the Weyl module of $S(d,n)$ for a partition $\lambda\vdash n$ with at most $d$ parts. For a composition $\mu$ of $n$ of length $d$, let $G^\lambda_\mu$ be the Gram determinant of its $\mu$-weight space in the semistandard basis ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Here $\operatorname{last}(T)$ is the least-dominant standardization in the fiber of $T$, and $d_\mu$ is the exact alternating semistandard number of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. **Both beta shifts use the same removed hook length $h_{ac}$.**

The exponent is the sorting sign times $|T_0(\eta,\mu)|$ if that balanced beta sequence has distinct nonnegative entries and recovers $\eta$; it is zero otherwise. Equivalently, remove the rim strip $R_{ac}$ and rewrap its $h_{ac}$ boxes with lowest node in column $b$. The sign is the parity of the heights of the removed strip and the newly added strip, the latter measured in the new diagram $\eta$; it is not generally the sum of two old $\lambda$ hook legs ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]], [[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]).

Over $R$ the formula means the specialization of that Laurent polynomial. It does not require inverting a vanishing hook number or evaluating $0/0$. All weights and $d<n$ are retained; an empty weight space has determinant $1$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The normalized semistandard maps, weight projections and Weyl cell form of the q-Schur Definition; the beta symbols and branching identity; and the hook-to-bead-gap correspondence in the cited suppliers.

[F1] The ordinary cell maps have the normalization $\varphi_{ST}(m_\nu h)=m_{ST}h$, with $m_{ST}=\sum_{\mu(s)=S,\nu(t)=T}m_{st}$. Their star swaps the indices, and their four-index cell product defines the Weyl form ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). The actual regular corner identifies this product with the Murphy product with factor $1$ ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]).

[F2] Over $K=\mathbb Q(Q)$, the corrected intrinsic Murphy seminormal basis has its unitriangular normalization, adjacent-generator action and self-adjoint JM operators ([[thm-separated-hecke-residues-give-seminormal-idempotents-and-bases]]). For a semistandard $T$ and node $(i,j)$ of entry $v$, its predecessor set is precisely $$\Gamma_T(i,j)=\{(k,l):l<j,\ T(k,l)<v,\  T(k',l)>v\text{ for every }k'>k\}.$$ Equivalently $T(k,l)<v<T(k+1,l)$ with sentinel $+\infty$ below the column. Both inequalities are strict; an equal $v$ below excludes that column. Define $$\gamma_T:=\prod_{(i,j)}\prod_{(k,l)\in\Gamma_T(i,j)}  \frac{[j-i+k-l+1]_Q}{[j-i+k-l]_Q}.$$ The standard-tableau version is defined by the same rule.

[F3] The signed Kostka numbers satisfy $d_\mu(a)=\sum_{|C|=z}d_{\bar\mu}(a-\mathbf1_C)$, with zero values for repeated or negative beta entries ([[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Preserve small alphabets. Enlarge to $D=\max(d,n)$ temporarily. The sum of permutation summands with types supported on the first $d$ letters is a literal summand of the $D$-alphabet permutation module, with projection $p$ and $pS(D,n)p=S(d,n)$. The normalized maps whose two types have that support, their cell multiplication and their Weyl form coefficients are unchanged. Every semistandard shape with these types has at most $d$ rows. Thus proving the weight norm in the enlarged algebra, where the regular corner exists, proves the original norm as well. No hypothesis $d\ge n$ is added. [given, F1]

1.2 Compute the standard norms. For the canonical standard tableau, $\gamma_{t^\lambda}$ telescopes rowwise to $[\lambda]!_Q$, also its norm by $x_\lambda^2=[\lambda]!_Qx_\lambda$. If $s$ dominates $t=s(i,i+1)$, the adjacent action gives $f_t=f_s(T_i+\alpha)$ with $\alpha=1/[\rho]_Q$. Contravariance, orthogonality and the quadratic relation imply $\langle f_t,f_t\rangle=(Q+\alpha)(1-\alpha) \langle f_s,f_s\rangle$. The two swapped predecessor ratios give $\gamma_t=Q^{-1}(Q+\alpha)(1-\alpha)\gamma_s$: use $[\rho+1]=1+Q[\rho]$ and $[\rho-1]=Q^{-1}([\rho]-1)$. Increasing-length adjacent swaps of incomparable boxes reach every standard tableau, so $\langle f_t,f_t\rangle=Q^{\ell(d(t))}\gamma_t$. [F1, F2]

2.1 Compute the semistandard norms, including the missing scalar. Sums of JM elements over each label block commute with the corresponding row symmetrizer. Evaluation of the normalized map at $m_\mu$ gives their triangular action with leading eigenvalues $\sum_{T(i,j)=k}[j-i]_Q$. The joint eigenvalues distinguish $T$ over $K$: for every initial-label subshape they give its content multiset, whose diagonal counts determine the Young diagram. Finite triangular orthogonalization therefore gives $\psi_T=\varphi_T+$ more dominant terms. Let $U_T,V_T$ be the mutually adjoint cell maps between this weight and the regular weight, and let $\pi_t$ be the product of the axial ratios at standard predecessors with the **same** $T$-entry. Evaluation at $m_\mu$ gives $V_Tf_t=\pi_t\psi_T$: at the first standardization its scalar is the factorial of the row-intersection subgroup, also the telescoped $\pi_t$; an adjacent swap within a label block multiplies both scalars by $Q+\alpha$, since that row symmetrizer has $T_i$-eigenvalue $Q$. Finite bubble sorting connects the standardizations, proving the scalar for every $t$ in the fiber. For $t=\operatorname{last}(T)$, the strict boundary in [F2] partitions the standard predecessor set into $\Gamma_T$ and these same-entry predecessors, so $\gamma_t=\pi_t\gamma_T$. Also $U_T\psi_T$ has leading coefficient $1$ at $f_t$, all other terms more dominant, by the normalized map and the unitriangular basis changes. Hence adjointness gives $$\pi_t\langle\psi_T,\psi_T\rangle  =\langle f_t,U_T\psi_T\rangle  =Q^{\ell(d(t))}\gamma_t,$$ so $\langle\psi_T,\psi_T\rangle=Q^{\ell(d(t))}\gamma_T$. The transition determinant is $1$, yielding $G^\lambda_\mu=Q^N g^\lambda_\mu$ with $g^\lambda_\mu=\prod_T\gamma_T$. No norm is replaced by $Q^{\ell}$ alone. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 Prove the normalized beta product at the level of formal exponents. For $h\ge1$ put $$A_h(\beta,\mu)=-\sum_{b\ne c,\ \beta_b-h<\beta_c}  d_\mu(\beta-h\mathbf e_b+h\mathbf e_c).$$ A nonzero term requires $0\le\beta_b-h$, so the product is finite. Repeated beta entries cancel by exchanging the equal indices; a negative entry cannot become a valid term because, if it is the receiver, the lowered donor is still smaller. Thus these invalid sequences contribute zero exponents. Delete the largest semistandard label, occurring $z$ times in column feet $C$, to get $\beta-\mathbf1_C,\bar\mu$. The strict predecessor boundary excludes every column also in $C$. Consequently the literal exponent $E_h$ in $g$ obeys $$E_h(\beta,\mu)=\sum_{|C|=z}E_h(\beta-\mathbf1_C,\bar\mu)  +\sum_{|C|=z}\sum_{b\notin C,c\in C}  (\mathbf1_{\beta_b-\beta_c+1=h}-\mathbf1_{\beta_b-\beta_c=h})  d_{\bar\mu}(\beta-\mathbf1_C).$$ The final sum is exactly the axial ratio contributed by each deleted largest-label box. [F2, F3, step 2.1]

4.1 Verify the same recurrence for $A_h$. Apply [F3] to its summands and compare with $\sum_C A_h(\beta-\mathbf1_C,\bar\mu)$. Set $\delta=\beta_b-\beta_c-h$. The original condition is $\delta<0$ and the deleted one $\delta-\mathbf1_C(b)+\mathbf1_C(c)<0$. They differ only when $b\in C,c\notin C,\delta=0$ or $b\notin C,c\in C,\delta=-1$. In the first case, exchanging the two shifted beta entries turns the contribution into $-d_{\bar\mu}(\beta-\mathbf1_{C'})$ with $C'=C-b+c$, giving the negative term of step 3.1. In the second case, the exchanged entries give $+d_{\bar\mu}(\beta-\mathbf1_C)$, giving its positive term. Every other case cancels. At degree $0$ both exponent families vanish: a nonzero shifted empty beta sequence would have to exchange two entries with $h=\beta_b-\beta_c$, excluded by the strict condition. Induction gives $E_h=A_h$ and therefore $$g^\lambda_\mu=  \prod_{h\ge1}\prod_{b\ne c,\ \beta_b-h<\beta_c}  [h]_Q^{-d_\mu(\beta-h\mathbf e_b+h\mathbf e_c)}.$$ This proves the regrouping without copying the inconsistent signs in the printed display. [F3, step 3.1]

5.1 Convert to hooks. A surviving lowered bead $\beta_b-h$ is a nonnegative gap, so the bead-gap correspondence makes $h=h_{ab}$ for a node $(a,b)$. The remaining condition $\beta_c>\beta_b-h_{ab}=n-1-\lambda_a+a$ is equivalent to $c\le\lambda_a$; the paired nodes therefore lie in the same row. For $b<c$ write $h=h_{ab}$ and $k=h_{ac}$. Since $h-k=\beta_b-\beta_c$, the two ordered displaced sequences $\beta-h\mathbf e_b+h\mathbf e_c$ and $\beta-k\mathbf e_c+k\mathbf e_b$ exchange their two changed entries. Their signed numbers are negatives of each other, and their factors are exactly $([h]_Q/[k]_Q)^{d_\mu(\beta+k\mathbf e_b-k\mathbf e_c)}$. This proves the stated balanced hook product. Removing and rewrapping the $k$-strip is precisely this bead transfer; sorting counts its crossings, which are the heights of the removed and **new** strips. Colliding or negative sequences vanish by definition. [given, F3, step 4.1]

6.1 Specialize integrally. The semistandard form matrix has entries in $\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$, so its determinant and $Q^{-N}G^\lambda_\mu$ are Laurent polynomials. Steps 2.1-3.1 identify the rational products with these same polynomials in $\mathbb Q(Q)$. Base change of the free semistandard basis and its form now proves the identity over the given domain, including singular specializations and weights of dimension zero. No individual vanishing ratio is evaluated. All constructions are finite; no choice principle is used. [given, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1] ∎

For every $e_q$-restricted $\nu\vdash n$, $$[W^\lambda:L^\nu]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):D_{\mathrm M}(\nu)].$$

In the page's ordinary Dipper–James normalization ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]), these identities become $$\mathcal F(W^{\lambda'})\cong(S^\lambda)^\theta,\qquad \mathcal F(L^{\lambda'})\cong(D^\lambda)^\theta.$$ The latter module is nonzero exactly for $e_q$-regular $\lambda$ and is zero otherwise. For $e_q$-regular $\nu$, $$[W^{\lambda'}:L^{\nu'}]=[S^\lambda:D^\nu].$$ The accepted ordinary polytabloid comparison identifies $S^\lambda$ with the historical DJ module $P(\lambda)$ and identifies their form radicals through an explicit unit factor. Thus the dictionary concerns the actual ordinary modules, not merely a renamed cell module. A zero Hecke cell-form quotient is not asserted to be its actual module head. No semisimplicity or choice principle is assumed, and $n=0$ is included.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field, parameter, stable range and modules in the Statement; all modules are right modules and multiplication in $S=\operatorname{End}_H(M)$ is ordinary composition $(fg)(x)=f(g(x))$.

[F1] The actual projection $e$ onto $M^\omega=H$, for $\omega=(1^n,0^{d-n})$, satisfies $e^2=e$ and $eSe\cong H$ by left multiplication $\rho(h)(a)=ha$. The functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ ([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]).

[F2] The legitimate semistandard cellular construction is supported from $M^{\operatorname{type}(T)}$ to $M^{\operatorname{type}(S)}$ and sends its generating $m_{\operatorname{type}(T)}h$ to $m_{ST}h$; its star swaps $S,T$ and its right-cell coefficients fix the first index modulo higher shapes. The Weyl cell basis is $(w_T)_T$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Only the actual summand projections are weight idempotents; no assertion that all diagonal cellular elements are idempotent is used.

[F3] The independent Murphy cellular datum uses $m_{st}=T_{d(s)}^*x_\lambda T_{d(t)}$, with its higher ideal $I^{\rhd\lambda}$, right cell basis $(c_t)_t$ and form $G_\lambda$ characterized by $m_{as}m_{tb}\equiv G_\lambda(c_s,c_t)m_{ab}$ modulo that ideal ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]).

[F4] The nonzero cell-form quotients are pairwise distinct absolutely irreducible modules; when the form is not identically zero its radical is the unique maximal submodule. The Murphy quotient $D_{\mathrm M}(\nu)$ is nonzero precisely for $e_q$-restricted $\nu$ ([[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]], [[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]], [[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]).

[F5] The genuine ordinary bridge gives $P(\alpha)\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\alpha')^\theta$ and an explicit unit-scaled form identity, hence $D_{\mathrm{DJ}}(\alpha)\cong D_{\mathrm M}(\alpha')^\theta$ including zero quotients. This is the page's signed Specht normalization, and $\theta$ is an involutive algebra automorphism whose pullback is exact ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]], [[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Under [F1], $\rho(h)\rho(k)=\rho(hk)$ because both act on $H$ by left multiplication, so the identification uses $H$, without an opposite algebra. The functor $X\mapsto Xe$ is exact: for a short exact sequence, a lift $x$ of an element $y\in X''e$ yields the lift $xe$, and an element in the kernel lies in $X'$ and is fixed by $e$, hence lies in $X'e$. The tensor description uses the $(S,eSe)$-bimodule $Se$, which is a direct summand as a left $S$-module. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The support in [F2] gives $e\varphi_{ST}e=\delta_{\operatorname{type}(S),\omega}\delta_{\operatorname{type}(T),\omega}\varphi_{ST}$ and $w_Te=\delta_{\operatorname{type}(T),\omega}w_T$. Semistandard tableaux of type $\omega$ have each label once and are exactly standard tableaux. For standard $s,t$, their defining sum $m_{st}$ has one term, so $\varphi_{st}|_H(a)=m_{st}a$ and $\rho^{-1}(\varphi_{st})=m_{st}$. Thus the higher Schur ideal cuts out exactly $I^{\rhd\lambda}$ in the corner. Read the Schur right-cell law with first index any standard tableau of type $\omega$; coefficient independence permits this choice. Restricting the multiplication by $\rho(h)$ to $H$ gives $m_{st}h$, so its coefficients are the Murphy right-cell coefficients. Consequently $\Psi_\lambda:W^\lambda e\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, $w_t\mapsto c_t$, is an $H$-isomorphism. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 By the Schur cell product, $\varphi_{as}\varphi_{tb}\equiv B_\lambda(w_s,w_t)\varphi_{ab}$ modulo higher Schur shapes, with coefficient independent of the outer indices. Choose all four indices standard of shape $\lambda$ and type $\omega$. They lie in $eSe$; applying $\rho^{-1}$, or evaluating their endomorphisms at $1\in H$, gives $m_{as}m_{tb}\equiv B_\lambda(w_s,w_t)m_{ab}$ modulo $I^{\rhd\lambda}$. The unique coefficient in [F3] is $G_\lambda(c_s,c_t)$, proving $B_\lambda|_{W^\lambda e}=\Psi_\lambda^*G_\lambda$ exactly, with factor $1$. [F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Since $e^*=e$, contravariance gives $B_\lambda(xe,y(1-e))=B_\lambda(x,y(1-e)e)=0$. The decomposition $W^\lambda=W^\lambda e\oplus W^\lambda(1-e)$ is therefore orthogonal. A vector in $W^\lambda e$ pairs trivially with its complement, so it is in the restricted form radical exactly when it lies in $\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}W^\lambda$. Since the latter is an $S$-submodule, $\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}(W^\lambda e)=(\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}W^\lambda)e$. This holds even if the corner form is identically zero. [F2, step 3.1, algebra]

Exactness, step 4.1 and step 3.1 give $L^\lambda e\cong W^\lambda e/(\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}W^\lambda)e\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)/\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)=D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, including when this corner quotient is zero. [F2, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

The remaining factors are the distinct nonzero Murphy simples in [F4], giving $[W^\lambda:L^\nu]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):D_{\mathrm M}(\nu)]$ for each $e_q$-restricted $\nu$. No multiplicity preservation is asserted for a killed simple label. [F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 5.1, algebra]

Twisting both modules by the same exact equivalence preserves composition multiplicities, so step 6.1 gives $[W^{\lambda'}:L^{\nu'}]=[S^\lambda:D^\nu]$ for regular $\nu$. The genuine unit-scaled ordinary form bridge in [F5] also identifies these with the historical DJ polytabloid modules and quotients. At $n=0$, $e=1$ and each form has value $1$, so the same proof includes the empty partition. [F4, F5, step 2.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Separated Hecke residues give seminormal idempotents and bases
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, let $e=e(F,q)$ and assume $e>n$ (with $e=\infty$ allowed); let $\lambda\vdash n$, $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$, and let $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ be the Murphy cell module with Murphy basis $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).

1. (**Separation**) If $s,t$ are standard $\lambda$-tableaux with $[\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$ for all $1\le k\le n$ then $s=t$. More precisely, if the q-content values agree for all $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$ for some $i$, then $s=t$ or $t=s(i\ i+1)$. 2. (**Idempotents**) Let $\mathcal R_k$ be the set of distinct q-content values of the entry $k$ over standard tableaux of **all** partitions of $n$. For a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ define $$F_t:=\prod_{k=1}^{n}\ \prod_{\substack{c\in\mathcal R_k\\        c\ne[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q}}        \frac{L_k-c}{[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q-c}\in F[L_1,\ldots,L_n].$$ These are orthogonal idempotents of $H$; their actions on $S_{\mathrm M}^\lambda$ project onto the corresponding simultaneous eigenlines. Put $f_t=m_tF_t$. Then $f_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_qf_t$ and $f_t=m_t+\sum_{s\rhd t}a_sm_s$. The global content sets are essential for the asserted idempotency in $H$, rather than only the induced same-shape endomorphisms. 3. (**Orthogonal seminormal basis**) $\{f_t:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is a basis of $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ satisfying $f_tF_s=\delta_{ts}f_t$ and $\langle f_s,f_t\rangle_\lambda=\delta_{st}\langle f_t,f_t\rangle_\lambda$; it is the **seminormal basis** of the Murphy cell module. 4. (**Generator action**) Let $s$ be a standard $\lambda$-tableau, $1\le i<n$ and $t:=s(i\ i+1)$, and put $\rho:=\operatorname{content}_s(i)-\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)\in\mathbb Z$. If $i$ and $i+1$ lie in the same row of $s$ then $f_sT_i=q\,f_s$; if they lie in the same column then $f_sT_i=-f_s$; otherwise $t$ is standard and $$f_sT_i=\alpha_i(s)\,f_t-\frac{1}{[\rho]_q}f_s,\qquad \alpha_i(s):=\begin{cases}1,&s\rhd t,\\[1mm]\dfrac{[1+\rho]_q[1-\rho]_q}{[\rho]_q[-\rho]_q},&t\rhd s,\end{cases}$$ where $[-\rho]_q$ is the extended quantum integer of [[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]] and for the swapped tableau $\operatorname{content}_t(i)-\operatorname{content}_t(i+1)=-\rho$. No semisimplicity of $H$ is assumed and no choice principle is used.
